slides.title: Python as a calculator
slides.content: Python as a calculator • Computers are very good at number-crunching • Operators (specially reserved symbols) represent mathematical computations: Addition 3 + 2 Subtraction 5 - 1 Multiplication 4 * 5 Division 20 / 2 Exponentiation 10 ** 2 Modulus 100 % 8 Floor division 4 // 3 • The values the operator is applied to are called operands 2/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Python as a calculator
slides.content: Python as a calculator One or more operators can be used to form an expression In: 1 + 2 * 3 Out: 7 In: (1 + 2) * 3 Out: 9 3/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Python as a calculator
slides.content: Python as a calculator One or more operators can be used to form an expression In: 1 + 2 * 3 Out: 7 In: (1 + 2) * 3 Out: 9 Note: • Python follows the precedence rules of mathematics (exponentiation before multiplication/division before addition/subtraction) • Parentheses can be used to specify a different order 3/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Numeric data types
slides.content: Numeric data types • Values have a type • Different types for numeric values: Integers (whole numbers): 1, 2, 3, …, -1, -2, -3 Floating point numbers: 2.5, 1.3333, … 4/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Numeric data types
slides.content: Numeric data types • Values have a type • Different types for numeric values: Integers (whole numbers): 1, 2, 3, …, -1, -2, -3 Floating point numbers: 2.5, 1.3333, … In: 5 / 2 Out: 2.5 In: type(5 / 2) Out: float In: type(5 // 2) Out: int 4/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Variables
slides.content: Variables • A variable is a name that refers to a value • A variable can be used to store the result of an expression so that it can be re-used • A variable is created/updated using the equal sign (‘=’) In: a = 5 / 2 In: a Out: 2.5 • Name of the variable: • can be arbitrarily long • can contain both letters and numbers, but cannot start with a number • may also contain underscore character • is case-sensitive 5/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Terminology
slides.content: Terminology Constant e.g., 2, 5, 1.5, … Expression A sequence of operands (constants) and operators • 2 + 5 • 1 + 2 + 3 • etc. Variable a container that holds a value, can be used in place of constants; e.g., a, b, books, … 6/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Using variables
slides.content: Using variables We can use a variable in expressions instead of a constant: In: a + 0.5 Out: 3.0 7/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Using variables
slides.content: Using variables We can use a variable in expressions instead of a constant: In: a + 0.5 Out: 3.0 A program is executed line-by-line, and variables can be overwritten: In: a = 2 In: a Out: 2 In: a = 3 In: a Out: 3 7/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Updating variables
slides.content: Updating variables A common operation is to increase the value of a variable: In: a = 2 In: a = a + 1 Out: 3 8/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Updating variables
slides.content: Updating variables A common operation is to increase the value of a variable: In: a = 2 In: a = a + 1 Out: 3 There is a shorthand for this operation: In: a = 2 In: a += 1 Out: 3 Also -=, *=, etc. 8/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: An example: Reading Proust
slides.content: An example: Reading Proust How many months does it take me to read all seven volumes of Marcel Proust’s novel À la recherche du temps perdu (In Search of Lost Time)? • Number of words in La Recherche: 1,267,069 • Time spent reading per day: 1 hour • Number of words per minute: 238 How to calculate the total reading time in months? 9/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Text
slides.content: Text Values can also be text instead of numbers: author = 'Marcel Proust' movie = "Breakfast at Tiffany's" lyrics = """When I find myself in times of trouble Mother Mary comes to me Speaking words of wisdom, let it be""" • A string (str, short for string of characters) is the type used for text • Single quotes, double quotes, or three quotation marks for different usages 10/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Types
slides.content: Types • We have seen numbers (int, float) and text (str) • These are examples of types • A type is a class of values recognized by the language • In Python, a value always has a type (a variable can be any type) • The type determines what operations are valid 11/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Different behavior for types
slides.content: Different behavior for types In: 3 + 3 Out: 6 These are numbers, so we can do arithmetic In: '3' + '3' Out: '33' These are strings, so they are treated as text 12/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Invalid operations for types
slides.content: Invalid operations for types In: 3 + '3' Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str' 13/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Converting numbers to text and back
slides.content: Converting numbers to text and back In: number = 42 In: text = str(number) In: text Out: '42' In: int(text) Out: 42 • str(number) and int(text) are examples of using a function • A function is a piece of code that can be invoked by name • It may take input (arguments) • It may produce output (return value) • The notation f(x) means that the function f is applied to the value x 14/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary • Values and types: Numbers: int, float Text: str • Expressions: 1 + 2 * 3 - (4 + 5) • Variables: a = 2 • Functions: str(2), int('2') 15/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Comments
slides.content: Comments • Large piece of code can be difficult to read • It helps to explain what you’re doing • Explanations are called comments • Comments start with hash (#) • Everything behind the # is ignored by the Python interpreter c = (f - 32) * (5/9) 16/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Comments
slides.content: Comments • Large piece of code can be difficult to read • It helps to explain what you’re doing • Explanations are called comments • Comments start with hash (#) • Everything behind the # is ignored by the Python interpreter temp_c = (temp_f - 32) * (5/9) #convert fahrenheit to celsius 16/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Example: computing readability
slides.content: Example: computing readability • Automated readability index • A formula to estimate the difficulty of a text 0.50( total words total sentences) + 4.71(total characters total words ) −21.43 • Result: a grade level, e.g. • 1 = kindergarten, age 5 • 14 = college student, age 18 17/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be Smith & Senter (1968). Automated readability index. https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/667273.pdf

slides.title: Indexing: extracting one element
slides.content: Indexing: extracting one element In: name = 'Marcel' In: name[0] Out: 'M' In: name[-1] Out: 'l' • a[n] gets the n’th character of a • Counting starts at zero • negative indices start from the end • -1 for last character • -2 second to last • etc. 18/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Slicing: extracting a range of elements
slides.content: Slicing: extracting a range of elements In: name = 'Marcel' In: name[1:3] Out: 'ar' In: name[:2] Out: 'Ma' In: name[1:] Out: 'arcel' • a[n:m] extracts characters n to m • Counting starts at zero • Result is up to but not including character m (half-open interval) • if n or m is left out, beginning or end is used 19/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Indexing and slicing
slides.content: Indexing and slicing 20/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Length
slides.content: Length Get the number of characters in a string: In: name = 'Marcel' In: len(name) Out: 6 21/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Functions
slides.content: Functions We have seen a number of functions: • int() • print() • len() • Reminder: • A function is a piece of code that can be invoked by name • It may take input (arguments): len(name) • It may produce a result: len(name) or an effect: print('hello', name) • The notation f(x) means that the function f is applied to the value x • The functions above are builtin functions: they are defined by default by the Python interpreter • You can also define your own functions (more on that later) 22/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Format strings
slides.content: Format strings In: x = 1 In: y = 2 In: z = x + y How to combine text and variables in a message? In: print('The sum of ' + str(x) + ' and ' + str(y) + ' is ' + str(z) + The sum of 1 and 2 is 3. In: print('The sum of', x, 'and', y, 'is', z, '.') The sum of 1 and 2 is 3 . 23/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Format strings
slides.content: Format strings In: x = 1 In: y = 2 In: z = x + y How to combine text and variables in a message? In: print('The sum of ' + str(x) + ' and ' + str(y) + ' is ' + str(z) + The sum of 1 and 2 is 3. In: print('The sum of', x, 'and', y, 'is', z, '.') The sum of 1 and 2 is 3 . Or using a formatted string: In: print(f'The sum of {x} and {y} is {z}.') The sum of 1 and 2 is 3. 23/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sequences
slides.content: Sequences • A string is a kind of sequence consisting of characters • A sequence contains elements in a particular order • Basic operations on sequences: length: len(seq) indexing: seq[index] slicing: seq[start:end] concatenation: seq1 + seq2 repetition: seq * num 24/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Lists
slides.content: Lists • Lists are sequences that may contain any kind of value as items In: numbers = [0, 1, 2] In: names = ['John', 'Mary'] 25/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: List indexing
slides.content: List indexing 26/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Changing items
slides.content: Changing items In: names = ['John', 'Mary'] In: names[1] = 'Alice' In: names Out: ['John', 'Alice'] • But: characters in a string cannot be changed • Necessary to create a new string In: name = 'Maria' In: name[0] = 'D' TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment • Why? Lists are mutable, strings are immutable • immutable objects do not allow modification after creation 27/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Immutable vs. mutable
slides.content: Immutable vs. mutable Immutable • Sometimes we want to ensure objects cannot be changed • Immutable objects are quicker to access Mutable • Size and content of objects can be changed • More efficient if we need to change/update the contents 28/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Objects and their methods
slides.content: Objects and their methods • In Python, every value is an object • An object encapsulates data and code for dealing with that data • A function that belongs to and operates on an object is called a method Regular function: function(argument) Method of object: obj.function(argument) 29/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Adding items
slides.content: Adding items • We can add an item to the end of an existing list: In: names = ['John', 'Mary'] In: names.append('Alice') In: names Out: ['John', 'Mary', 'Alice'] • We can combine two lists into a new list: In: friends = ['John', 'Mary'] In: enemies = ['Alice', 'Bob'] In: friends + enemies Out: ['John', 'Mary', 'Alice', 'Bob'] • Note: append mutates the list, + only creates a new list 30/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Removing items
slides.content: Removing items • remove(elem) looks for the first occurrence of elem and removes it from the list In: names = ['John', 'Mary'] In: names.remove('John') In: names Out: ['Mary'] • .pop(value) removes the item at position value and returns it • .pop() (without argument) removes the last items and returns it In: names = ['John', 'Mary', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Max'] In: names.pop(3) # removes 4th item Out: 'Bob' In: names.pop() # removes last item Out: 'Max' In: names Out: ['John', 'Mary', 'Alice'] 31/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Removing items (2)
slides.content: Removing items (2) • We can also use slicing to keep a part of a list In: names = ['John', 'Mary', 'Alice', 'Bob'] In: friends = names[:2] In: friends Out: ['John', 'Mary'] 32/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sorting
slides.content: Sorting In: letters = ['b', 'd', 'a', 'c'] In: letters Out: ['b', 'd', 'a', 'c'] In: sorted(letters) Out: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] In: letters Out: ['b', 'd', 'a', 'c'] In: letters.sort() In: letters Out: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] • The function sorted() leaves the original list unchanged and returns the sorted result • The method .sort() modifies the list itself, and does not return anything 33/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Nested lists: lists inside of lists
slides.content: Nested lists: lists inside of lists In: ages = [['John', 34], ['Mary', 19], ['Max', 62]] • How to access elements? In: name_and_age = ages[0] In: name_and_age Out: ['John', 34] In: name_and_age[1] Out: 34 34/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Nested lists: lists inside of lists
slides.content: Nested lists: lists inside of lists In: ages = [['John', 34], ['Mary', 19], ['Max', 62]] • How to access elements? In: name_and_age = ages[0] In: name_and_age Out: ['John', 34] In: name_and_age[1] Out: 34 In: ages[0][1] Out: 34 34/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Nested lists: lists inside of lists
slides.content: Nested lists: lists inside of lists In: ages = [['John', 34], ['Mary', 19], ['Max', 62]] • How to access elements? In: name_and_age = ages[0] In: name_and_age Out: ['John', 34] In: name_and_age[1] Out: 34 In: ages[0][1] Out: 34 34/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Summary: strings vs lists
slides.content: Summary: strings vs lists Both strings and lists are sequences: • Items in a fixed order • Has a length • Can extract items or slices Two important differences: 1 lists are more general than strings • Strings always consist of characters • Lists can consist of any data types / objects 2 Lists are mutable and strings are immutable 35/36 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
